title: I Quit Teaching
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. tells the story of how he functionally quit teaching after three intense, effort-driven years in Baltimore. He had leaned on a random grab bag of tricks and a savior-teacher mindset, and when he moved to New York he drifted toward writing and seminary without admitting he had left the classroom. Returning to Michigan with a growing family, he discovered that his Baltimore tactics did not transfer and that he lacked any coherent understanding of the few things that matter most in teaching. The post is a candid account of how unsustainable, incoherent teaching practice pushes capable people out of the profession, and it ends on the choice that something had to change. It sets up the series that follows.
points: Early-career effort without a coherent framework produces a bag of tricks that fails the moment the context changes.
The savior-teacher self-image, 'Dave-centric' rather than professional, makes even a triumphant moment a prelude to leaving.
Quitting can be functional rather than declared: Stuart drifted away from teaching for a year without saying so.
Becoming a husband and father exposed that a work-every-night model of teaching is not sustainable.
quotes: I had no coherent understanding of my work, no transferable sense of the few things that mattered most, regardless of course details or grade level or curriculum.
Looking back, I see myself guessing at just about everything, making up for a lack of understanding with an abundance of effort.
I was still pretty chained to a Dave-centric way of thinking about the work — teacher as savior versus teacher as professional — so it was a hugely gratifying moment.
I still wasn’t telling myself that I had quit teaching. But I had. Functionally, I had quit.

You can see why, even in those early months as a Cedar Springs High School long-term sub, I wasn’t planning on sticking around in teaching. It wasn’t sustainable. It didn’t make sense. It was frustrating.
Most of the tactics I used in Baltimore didn’t work — mostly because they were just a random grab bag of tricks and tips.
